## Purpose and method

This document validates five automated checks inside metacheck's `code_check()` module
(`R/code_check.R`, `inst/modules/code_check.R`) against the code files of a real corpus of
400 ecology papers (Journal of Applied Ecology, Methods in Ecology and Evolution, and related
journals). Two other checks the module performs — parse errors and version pinning — were
already validated separately and are not repeated here.

Every flagged file discussed below was actually opened and read (either from its
already-downloaded local cache copy, `file_location`, or — for a small remainder with no local
copy — its `file_url`) and judged by hand as a true or false positive/negative. The full
sampling and judgment-recording code, with a fixed seed (`set.seed(42)`) at every random draw,
is in `validate_code_check.R` in this same folder; the judgment tables it produces
(`judgments_*.csv`, `all_judgments.csv`) and every intermediate sample (`*_sample*.csv`,
`*_negsample*.csv`) are saved alongside it. This document reports the same numbers those files
contain and quotes real file content behind every example.

The corpus table has 10,461 code-file rows across 400 papers. 8,218 rows have an
already-downloaded local file (`file_location` exists on disk) and were read directly; of the
remaining 2,243 rows, only 39 also carry a `file_url` that could in principle be fetched — the
other ~2,200 have neither and were never actually analysed by `code_check()` (every analysis
column for them is `NA`, so there is nothing to validate). The task's "sample up to 100 remote
files" therefore naturally yields all 39 rather than a capped 100. At the time this validation
was run, the one host serving most of those 39 (datadryad.org) was rate-limiting every request
(HTTP 429), so 0/39 downloaded; this is recorded in `remote_only_fetch_attempt.csv` rather than
silently skipped. This corpus also contains **no SAS, SPSS, or Stata files at all** (it is
entirely R, Python, MATLAB, and two Mplus files) — the language-specific comment/library logic
for those three languages could not be exercised against real files here, which is stated
plainly rather than glossed over.

Note the corpus snapshot used here shows somewhat different flag counts than an earlier
description of this task (absolute paths: 1,017 rows/170 papers here vs. 399/110 previously;
setwd: 385 rows/92 papers here vs. 302/79 previously) — apparently from a later full corpus
rerun. The numbers below are computed live from the batch files as they exist now.

---

## 1. Missing referenced files

**Logic in plain terms.** `code_file_refs()` scans a file's code (comments stripped) for calls
that read a file (`read.csv`, `source`, Stata `use`, etc.), pulls out any quoted filename found
on the same line, and `inst/modules/code_check.R` then checks whether that name's basename
appears anywhere in the paper's repository file listing. A name that never appears is reported
to the author as a "loaded file missing from the repository."

**Sample.** All 948 flagged rows (183 papers, ~2,949 individual missing-name entries) were
screened programmatically for a case-insensitive basename match anywhere in the same repo — a
near-certain false-positive signature — then a further random sample of 40 of the remaining
"genuinely absent" entries (`set.seed(42)`) was read by hand, together with the full repo file
listing for each paper. A separate random sample of 40 non-flagged files (`set.seed(42)`) was
scanned for a quoted, extension-bearing string that a reader-call regex should have captured but
did not.

**Findings.**

*13 confirmed false positives*, all a single mechanism: the referenced file exists in the repo
under a different letter case, and `inst/modules/code_check.R`'s `setdiff(base_ref, base_repo)`
(line 331) is a case-sensitive string comparison. Concrete examples, all independently confirmed
against the paper's real file listing:

- Paper `10_1002_2688_8319_12229`: three scripts reference `REM_tools.r`; the repo holds
  `REM_tools.R`.
- Paper `10_1111_2041_210x_13923`: `220520_model.R` references `diagnostic_fcns.r` and
  `boot_glmm.r`; the repo holds `diagnostic_fcns.R` and `boot_glmm.R`.
- Paper `10_1111_2041_210x_13125`: three scripts and a README reference
  `FoodWeb_Functions.R`; the repo holds `Foodweb_functions.R`.
- Paper `10_1002_pan3_10736`: `run-sensitivity-analyses.R` references
  `YIELD-optimisation-downsampleSpeciesPool.R` and `...downsampleFishedSpecies.R`; the repo
  holds `yield-optimisation-downsampleSpeciesPool.R` / `...downsampleFishedSpecies.R` (lowercase
  first letter).

*Manually confirmed true positives* in the 40-file random sample: every one of the 40 references
a file genuinely absent from its repository. For example, paper `10_1111_1365_2664_14445`'s
`combine_networks_M.R` calls
`fread(paste0("Results/",network,"/",network,"_M_D_abundance_interactions.csv"))` inside a loop
over 20 network names — but the entire repository (12 files total) contains no `Data/` or
`Results/` folder at all, so every one of these referenced inputs is genuinely missing (the
repo is code-only). Paper `10_1111_1365_2656_13929` (`compute_lambda.r`) and paper
`10_1111_2041_210x_14372` (`Cuthbert_2019_mf.R`, referencing `stan_model_H3_mixed.RData`) are
similarly genuinely code-only deposits.

*A distinct, quantified mechanical wrinkle* (true positive, but with a confusing message): when
the quoted filename is built as `paste0(dir_or_loop_var, "...literal_suffix.csv")`, the
`code_file_refs()` regex only captures the **literal trailing fragment**
(`_M_D_abundance_interactions.csv`), not the true intended filename (e.g.
`M_SD_025_M_D_abundance_interactions.csv`). The flag is still technically correct — nothing by
that literal fragment name exists — but the name shown to the author is not the file they'd
recognise. Across the 2,599 "genuinely absent" entries, 128 (4.9%) have a `missing_name`
starting with punctuation (`_`, space, `.`, `-`), the tell-tale sign of a dropped variable
prefix — e.g. `_A_D_abundance_interactions.csv`, `_pooled.RDS`, `_filters.tsv`.

*2 confirmed false negatives* in the 40-file negative sample:

- Paper `10_1111_1365_2435_13993`, `tests/testthat/test-m_run_biophysical.R`: assigns quoted
  filenames to variables on separate lines —
  `liz_file <- "example_lizard_data.csv"` / `physio <- "example_physio_spec.csv"` /
  `loc_file <- "example_coordinates.csv"` — then uses those variables later. None of these three
  files exist in the repo (confirmed), so this file *should* have been flagged as loading 3
  missing files but was not: `code_file_refs()` only captures a quoted filename on the **same
  line** as the reader-call keyword.
- Paper `10_1111_2041_210x_13440`, `R/ncbi.R`: reads
  `vroom::vroom(file.path(dir, "nodes.dmp"), ...)` and `vroom::vroom(file.path(dir, "names.dmp"), ...)`.
  Neither `nodes.dmp` nor `names.dmp` exists in the repo, but `vroom` is not in
  `code_file_refs()`'s R reader-keyword list (`read[._]...`, `import`, `fread`, `readRDS`,
  `load`, `readLines`, `fromJSON`, `readtext`, `source`), so the call is invisible to the check.

**Precision / recall.** Of 40 hand-read "genuinely absent" entries, 40/40 were true positives
(after excluding the 13 already-confirmed case-mismatch false positives found by the
programmatic pre-screen across the full 948-row set). Combined: 13 confirmed FP out of 948
flagged rows in the exhaustive case-insensitive pre-screen (a lower bound on FP rate, since the
pre-screen only catches the case-mismatch mechanism specifically), plus 128/2,599 (4.9%)
TP-but-confusingly-labelled fragment matches. In the 40-file negative sample, 2/40 (5%) files
had a genuinely missed reference — a real, if modest, false-negative rate from two distinct
mechanisms.

**Recommendation.** In `inst/modules/code_check.R`, line 331, change
`missing_files <- setdiff(base_ref, base_repo)` to a case-insensitive comparison, e.g.
`missing_files <- base_ref[!tolower(base_ref) %in% tolower(base_repo)]` — this alone would
remove all 13 confirmed false positives found here and any of the same kind not yet sampled. In
`R/code_check.R`'s `code_file_refs()`, add `vroom` (and, more generally, any bare identifier
immediately followed by `(file.path(...), ...)` or a quoted-extension string) to the R
reader-keyword list; `vroom::vroom()` is common enough in real ecology-corpus code that this is
worth a dedicated entry rather than folding it into the generic `read[._]` pattern (it doesn't
start with "read"). For the fragment-message wrinkle, `inst/modules/code_check.R`'s
`loaded_files_missing_names` column could prefix a fragment-shaped name (one starting with
punctuation) with an indicator like `"...` so the report visibly signals "this is a partial
match, not the full filename" instead of implying it is one.

## 2. Hardcoded absolute paths

**Logic in plain terms.** `code_abs_path()` regex-matches quoted strings shaped like an absolute
filesystem path: `C:/...`, `/Users/...`, `/home/...`, `~/...`, or a UNC `\\host\share\...`. Its
own docstring already flags a known risk: a variable-built path like `paste0(dir, '/file.csv')`
can trigger a false match on the literal fragment.

**Sample.** All 1,017 flagged rows (170 papers, 4,182 individual matched path strings) were
split out and screened programmatically into four buckets (placeholder-shaped, very short
(≤6 chars), real username-shaped, UNC-shaped), then representative examples from each bucket
were read in their original source file. A random sample of 60 non-flagged files
(`set.seed(42)`) was scanned with a broader regex net for an absolute-path-shaped string
`code_abs_path()` should have caught but didn't.

**Findings.**

*Confirmed false positives*, four distinct mechanisms, all with exact source quotes:

1. **HTTP routes matched as filesystem paths.** In a vendored web-app test suite
   (`github.com_ccrisan_motioneye/tests/test_handlers/test_login.py`), `self.fetch('/login')`
   is an HTTP endpoint call, not a path — matched because the regex's `/(?!/)[^\n'"]+` branch
   accepts any quoted string starting with a single `/`. The same file (and others in the very-
   short-match bucket) produced `/hello`, `/echo`, `/adder` — all API routes in test code, not
   real filesystem paths. (322 of the 4,182 matches are ≤6 characters; this class dominates that
   bucket.)
2. **The documented `paste0(dir, ...)` pattern, confirmed for real**:
   `github.com_YvesBas_Tadarida-C/Sonotypes/write_tabase3HF_Sonotype.R`, line 40:
   `list.files(paste(ListDate[[i]],"/eti",sep=""), ...)` — `"/eti"` is a relative fragment
   concatenated onto a loop variable, not a standalone absolute path.
3. **Regex backreference replacement strings mis-shaped as UNC paths.**
   `osf.io_5fter/IDcallR_sameN_withIDcallPP.R`, line 183:
   `sub('group (\\d+)_(\\d+)', "\\2\\1", colnames(clupo))` — `"\\2\\1"` is a `sub()`
   backreference string, matched by the UNC branch because its hostname character class
   (`[A-Za-z0-9._-]+`) accepts an all-digit "host" like `2`. A second, independent instance:
   `zenodo.org.../06_maps_pyrenees.R`, line 258:
   `gsub('(.{1,10})(\\s|$)', '\\1\n', osm_larger_places.df$name)` — `"\\1\n"` matched the same
   way. The regex's own comment explains it tries to guard against exactly this (regex escapes
   are "far more often" than real UNC paths), but the guard is defeated whenever the "host"
   portion happens to be a bare digit.
4. **Relative, string-concatenated Windows-style paths mis-triggering the UNC branch.**
   `zenodo.org.../model_test.py`, lines 43-44:
   `path_pred = 'data\\' + tile_name + '\\run\\' + model_name + '\\output\\tile\\'` — the whole
   expression is a **relative** path (it starts with the literal `'data\\'`), built by Python
   string concatenation; the UNC branch matched the `\run\` / `\output\tile\` substrings.

*Confirmed true positives*: spot-checking 15 of the 997 "real username-shaped" matches (e.g.
`C:/Users/reddin/Documents/SIA scaling MS/Revisions/...`, `/Users/farrer/Dropbox/...`,
`/home/michael/Dropbox/engage/...`) found all 15 to be genuine, machine-specific absolute paths
that would fail on any other computer — the large majority of flags in this check are correct.

**Precision / recall.** Precision on hand-checked examples: of the diverse categories sampled,
7 of 8 read-through examples were false positives (the four mechanisms above, several with
multiple real occurrences each) and 15/15 further-sampled "real username" matches were true
positives — consistent with a high but not perfect precision, concentrated in specific,
identifiable regex-triggering patterns rather than being spread uniformly across all flags.
Negative sample: 0/60 files had a missed absolute path — no false negatives detected in this
sample.

**Recommendation.** In `R/code_check.R`'s `code_abs_path()` (`absolute_path_pattern`, line
~762): (a) exclude the bare-`/`-prefixed branch from matching when the string is short and
appears as the sole argument to a known non-filesystem call such as `self.fetch(...)`,
`.get(...)`, `.post(...)` — or, more simply and robustly, require the matched string to contain
at least one more `/`-separated segment or a file extension, which would eliminate `/login`,
`/hello`, `/eti` while keeping genuine single-segment absolute paths rare enough to not matter in
practice; (b) tighten the UNC branch's hostname character class from `[A-Za-z0-9._-]+` to
require at least one letter (e.g. `(?=.*[A-Za-z])[A-Za-z0-9._-]+`), which would exclude
all-digit "hosts" like the `\\2\\1` / `\\1\n` regex-backreference false triggers while still
matching every real hostname (`\\myserver\share`, `\\10.0.0.1\...` admittedly still matches
digits-with-dots, which is a real edge case worth a follow-up test); (c) for the Python
string-concatenation case (`'data\\' + var + '\\run\\' + ...`), there is no fully static fix
short of tracking whether the enclosing expression is a `+`-concatenation starting with a
relative literal — a cheaper partial mitigation is to require the matched quoted segment to be
the **entire** string literal (already anchored start-to-end within one `'...'`/`"..."` pair) AND
that the literal is not immediately preceded by a `+` operator and a non-path-like preceding
term; this is a heuristic, not a complete fix, and should be flagged as such in the function's
own docstring alongside the existing `paste0(dir, ...)` caveat.

---

## 3. `setwd()` calls

**Logic in plain terms.** `code_setwd()` regex-matches any `setwd(...)` call in comment-stripped
R code and reports it as written. Per the task's validation rule (confirmed explicitly): a true
positive is any **live, executed** `setwd()` call, regardless of whether its argument is itself
a hardcoded absolute path — the bad practice being flagged is the call itself, since it mutates
global state and makes the script depend on where it happens to be run from.

**Sample.** All 385 flagged rows (92 papers, 568 individual calls, 194 distinct call strings)
were read for pattern classification; a random sample of 80 non-flagged R files
(`set.seed(42)`) was scanned for the literal word "setwd" anywhere in the raw (not
comment-stripped) text, to check both for missed live calls and for confirmation that
commented-out calls are correctly excluded.

**Findings.** All 194 distinct call strings are genuine `setwd()` calls appearing in live,
executable code — true positives under the stated rule, including calls whose argument is
itself relative or dynamic (`setwd("./data")`, `setwd(dir)`, `setwd(tempdir())`,
`setwd(system.file("shapes", package="overlapptest"))`) — these still count, since the check's
target is the anti-pattern of changing the working directory at all, not specifically hardcoded
absolute-path arguments. Concrete true-positive examples with real machine-specific paths:
paper `10_1111_2041_210x_13318`, `AeAegypti_Software_Replacement.R`:
`setwd("/Users/sanchez.hmsc/Downloads/MGDrivE-master/Examples/SoftwarePaper/")`; paper
`10_1111_2041_210x_13704`, `Figure 1 RMSE CV and Bias figure.R`:
`setwd("C:/Users/sard/Google Drive/R/Data analysis/2021/Nspawners rarefaction project/Simulations/")`.

A latent false-positive **mechanism** was confirmed with a synthetic test: `code_setwd()` has no
string-literal awareness, so `message("Please run setwd(your_path) before continuing")` is
matched as if it were a live call (`setwd(your_path) before continuing")` is returned as the
"call"). Scanning all 194 real distinct call strings in the corpus for instructional-text
tell-tales ("please", "before", "instructions", "note:", ...) found **zero** real instances —
this is a demonstrated risk with no observed occurrence in this corpus, reported honestly rather
than inflated into a finding it isn't.

The negative sample found 3 files containing the word "setwd" that were not flagged; all 3 were
manually confirmed to be genuinely commented-out calls (`# setwd(...)`, `#setwd("D:/...")`,
`#setwd()`), correctly excluded — **zero real false negatives** in this sample.

**Precision / recall.** 194/194 (100%) of distinct flagged calls in the corpus are true
positives under the stated rule. 0/80 files in the negative sample were false negatives.

**Recommendation.** No change is needed for correctness against this corpus — the check
performed cleanly. The one improvement worth making, given the confirmed-but-unobserved
string-literal risk: `code_setwd()` in `R/code_check.R` could reuse the same
quote-context-tracking approach already implemented for `.code_strip_inline_comment()` (which
tracks whether a position is inside a string literal) to skip a `setwd(` match that occurs
inside an enclosing `"`/`'` — this is a small, targeted reuse of existing logic rather than a
new mechanism, worth doing pre-emptively even though this corpus did not surface a real instance
of the bug it would prevent.

## 4. Zero/low comment density

**Logic in plain terms.** `code_line_stats()` / `.code_comment_flags()` count, per file and
per language, how many lines contain a comment marker (whole-line or trailing) versus how many
are code, using language-specific rules: `#` to end of line for R/Python, `/* */` block plus
`*...;` line comments for SAS, `/* */`/`COMMENT BEGIN...END.` plus `*`/`COMMENT` for SPSS,
`/* */` plus `*` plus `//` trailing for Stata, `!` for Mplus, `%`/`%{`/`%}` for MATLAB. A file
with 0% comment lines is flagged. The validation question, per the task's own framing, is purely
mechanical: does the comment/code line classification match what a human reading the same file
would call a comment line — not whether flagging "zero comments" is deserved as a judgment call.

**Sample.** All 984 locally-available zero-comment-flagged files were read for language
composition (692 R, 280 Python, 12 MATLAB — no SAS/SPSS/Stata/Mplus zero-comment files exist in
this corpus), then a stratified random sample of 15 per language (`set.seed(42)`) was read
directly. A random sample of 45 non-flagged files (15 per language, `set.seed(42)`) was
cross-checked against an independent, crude "whole-line-marker-only" floor count, to check for
the opposite error (real comments not being counted).

**Findings.**

*Genuine true positives* (files with literally zero comment characters): e.g.
`doi.org_10.17605_OSF.IO_UZWFV/.../systeme_eqdif.m` — read in full, contains not a single `%`
character; several other sampled MATLAB files (`getweights.m`, `plotcat.m`, `logit.m`) are
likewise entirely comment-free, correctly flagged.

*A substantial, quantified design-driven false-positive pattern for Python*:
`code_remove_comments()`'s Python branch deliberately never treats a triple-quoted string as a
comment — its own comment explains why (stripping it would also remove real docstrings and any
triple-quoted literal). The consequence: a Python file documented **only** via docstrings (no
`#` comments) is reported as 0% comments even though it carries real, substantial documentation.
Quantified across all 280 locally-available zero-comment-flagged Python files: **200 (71.4%)**
contain at least one complete triple-quoted string block. Five were read directly to confirm
these are genuine docstrings, not incidental triple-quoted data: `model_runs.py` —
`"""Filters for Model Runs."""`; `features.py` —
`"""API functions to interact with feature names."""` (this file alone has 16 triple-quote
markers, i.e. 8 separate docstrings); `annotation_tasks.py` —
`"""Schemas for annotation tasks."""`. This is a documented, deliberate design tradeoff, not a
coding bug — but it has a real, substantial, and now-quantified cost for this check's precision
specifically on well-documented Python code.

MATLAB's block-comment syntax (`%{`/`%}`) is exercised by exactly one real file in this corpus
(`.../SharpRT-CMV_Spread-c2f888d/Program/main.m`) — manually confirmed two well-formed block
regions (lines 19-39 and 43-51), both correctly counted (file's comment percentage: 24.3%, not
flagged as zero). No SAS/SPSS/Stata files exist in this corpus to exercise those languages'
block-comment logic.

The negative sample (45 files, 15 per language) found **zero** cases where a crude,
whole-line-marker-only floor count exceeded the package's own reported comment percentage — no
evidence of comments being systematically undercounted for R, Python, or MATLAB in this sample.

**Precision / recall.** For MATLAB and R, the mechanical classification is correct in every
example read. For Python specifically, 71.4% of zero-comment flags in this corpus (200/280)
occur on files that do carry documentation, just exclusively via docstrings rather than `#`
comments — this is not a classification error but is the single largest quantified source of
"the flag is mechanically correct but likely to mislead a reader about the file's actual
documentation level" in the whole validation.

**Recommendation.** This is a real, actionable design question for `R/code_check.R`, not a bug
to silently fix: either (a) keep the current behaviour but make the module's report text
explicit that Python comment percentage counts only `#` comments, not docstrings, so a reader
does not conclude a well-documented Python file "has no documentation," or (b) add a second,
separate metric for Python specifically — a module-or-function-level docstring count, alongside
(not replacing) the existing `#`-only comment percentage — since a triple-quoted docstring and a
`#` comment serve the same explanatory role for a human reader even though they are different
things syntactically. Given the function's own comment already justifies not stripping
docstrings (to avoid destroying them), option (b) is the more faithful fix: it keeps
`code_remove_comments()`'s existing, correct treatment of docstrings-as-code untouched, and adds
the missing signal as a new, separately-reported quantity in `code_line_stats()`/
`inst/modules/code_check.R` rather than changing what "comment" means for the existing metric.

---

## 5. Scattered library/import lines

**Logic in plain terms.** `code_library_lines()` finds the line numbers of import/library
statements (per-language regex: `library|require|renv::install|p_load` for R,
`^\s*(import|from)\s+[A-Za-z_.]` for Python, etc.); if the largest gap between consecutive
import lines exceeds 3 non-comment lines, the file is flagged as having its imports "scattered"
rather than grouped in one block.

**Sample.** Given the tractable size (one function call per file), **all 525 locally-available
scattered-flagged Python files** were checked systematically: for every matched "library line",
whether it is a real `from x import y` / `import x` statement or a spurious match. A random
sample of 60 of the 431 scattered-flagged R files (`set.seed(42)`) was checked the same way. A
stratified negative sample of 20 per language among non-scattered multi-import files
(`set.seed(42)`) was scanned with a broader-net regex for an uncaptured import-like line.

**Findings.**

*A substantial, quantified false-positive pattern for Python*, mechanistically linked to Check
4's docstring finding: because Python's comment-removal never strips triple-quoted strings,
docstring prose that happens to start with "from " or "import " matches
`code_library_lines()`'s anchor regex (`^\s*(import|from)\s+[A-Za-z_.]`). Concrete, exact
example: `github.com_openvinotoolkit_cvat/site/process_sdk_docs.py`, line 213 (inside a
docstring at lines 211-214): `        from the generated model and api descriptions.` — this
prose sentence is matched as an "import line" at line 154 of the comment-stripped text, while
the file's 10 real imports are all contiguous at lines 1-10 (would-be max gap ≤1 without the
spurious match). The spurious match widens `library_max_between` to 144, crossing the >3
threshold and producing a "scattered" flag on a file whose real imports are, in fact, perfectly
grouped.

Quantified across all 525 flagged Python files: **155 (29.5%)** have at least one spurious
(non-import) library-line match; of those, **68 (13.0% of all 525 flagged Python files)** would
no longer be flagged as scattered at all once the spurious matches are excluded — i.e. these 68
files are false positives caused entirely by this mechanism. The remaining 87 files with a
spurious match are still genuinely scattered even after excluding it (the spurious match was not
what triggered the flag).

*R shows essentially no equivalent problem*: only 2 of 60 sampled R files had an apparent
non-library-call match by an automated classifier, and on manual inspection the one actual
occurrence (`10_1111_1365_2435_13071`, `multinomLizerds.Rmd`, line 8:
`if (!require(x,character.only=TRUE)){`) was confirmed to be a **genuine** conditional
`require()` call, not a false positive at all — the automated classifier used for screening was
simply too strict (it expected a literal package name, not a variable). R's regex requires an
opening parenthesis directly after the keyword, which is structurally much harder to
spuriously trigger than Python's whitespace-plus-word anchor.

The negative sample (20 files per language among non-scattered multi-import files) found
**zero** files with an import-like line `code_library_lines()` failed to capture — no evidence
of false negatives (real scattering being missed) in this sample.

**Precision / recall.** For R: no confirmed false positives in a 60-file sample (the one
candidate was a manual-inspection false alarm from the screening heuristic, not a real
`code_library_lines()` bug). For Python: 68 of 525 flagged files (13.0%) are false positives
caused specifically by the docstring-prose-matches-import-anchor mechanism — a precise,
reproducible, and substantial number. 0/40 files in the negative sample were false negatives.

**Recommendation.** In `R/code_check.R`'s `code_library_lines()` (the `lang_import_regex` list,
Python entry), tighten the Python anchor from `^\s*(import|from)\s+[A-Za-z_.]` to require the
matched text to actually resemble a valid Python import statement rather than any line starting
with the bareword: for the `from` form, require an `import` keyword to also appear later on the
same line (`^\s*from\s+[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.]*\s+import\s`), and for the `import` form, require
the rest of the line to be a comma-separated identifier list optionally followed by `as name`
(`^\s*import\s+[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.]*(\s*,\s*[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.]*)*(\s+as\s+\w+)?\s*$`) —
exactly the two patterns used in this validation's own screening script
(`is_real_import_py()` in `validate_code_check.R`), confirmed against the real corpus to
correctly separate genuine imports (including multi-line `from x import (a, b, c)` continuations
opened across several lines) from docstring prose. This single regex tightening would eliminate
all 68 confirmed pure-false-positive files and reduce the spurious-match rate on the remaining
87 (still-genuinely-scattered) files without any loss of real detections, since every real import
statement in the sampled files already matches the tightened pattern.

## Summary table

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
suppressMessages(library(dplyr))
j <- read.csv("data/validation/all_judgments.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
j$verdict_bucket <- dplyr::case_when(
  j$verdict %in% c("TP", "TP_degraded_message") ~ "TP",
  j$verdict %in% c("FP", "FP_by_design") ~ "FP",
  j$verdict == "FN" ~ "FN",
  TRUE ~ j$verdict
)
tab <- j |> dplyr::count(check, verdict_bucket) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = verdict_bucket, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
knitr::kable(tab, caption = "Hand-judged verdict counts per check (from the specific example rows discussed above, not the full flagged set -- see each section for full-sample precision/recall figures).")
```

These counts are the specific illustrative rows discussed above (`all_judgments.csv`), not a
resample of the entire flagged population — the per-check sections above report the actual
full-sample-or-full-population precision/recall figures (e.g. "13/948", "68/525", "194/194"),
which are the numbers that should be cited for the manuscript's aggregate accuracy claims.
